analysis.one_liner: Lets FDA approve competing generic drugs when the first generic filer stalls its launch.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in February 2025 and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company is first in line to sell a generic version of a brand-name drug, the FDA gives it 180 days of exclusive rights to that generic market. Sometimes that first company never actually starts selling — for example, after settling a patent lawsuit with the brand maker — which blocks every other generic maker from being approved. This bill would let the FDA approve a competing generic after 33 months if the first company has not launched, isn't blocked by patent claims, and another applicant certifies it can start selling within 75 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need drugs stuck behind a stalled first generic — their generic competition arrives years sooner, which usually means lower prices. Pharmacists, employers, and insurers that pay for prescriptions also benefit from more competition. Other generic manufacturers that are stuck waiting behind a first filer that never launched gain access to markets they are currently locked out of.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients waiting on stalled generic drugs

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, the first company to file for approval of a generic gets 180 days of market exclusivity, and the FDA generally cannot approve any competing generic while that company holds the right — even if it never starts selling the drug [S2].

The bill lets the FDA approve a competing generic applicant before the first filer launches, if five conditions are met: the application is ready for approval, the applicant certifies it can begin selling within 75 days, at least 33 months have passed since a first applicant filed, no patent infringement claim blocks the first filer's approval, and no first applicant has already been effectively approved [S2] [S3].

The bill includes enforcement teeth: a subsequent applicant that fails to start selling within 75 days of approval loses its approval and is barred from a later approval unless it certifies the failure was due to a genuinely unforeseen event that has since been resolved [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers lose some ability to extend a drug's monopoly by settling with a first generic filer that then sits on its 180-day exclusivity, and first-filer generic companies lose the ability to hold that exclusivity without launching. Taxpayers bear no direct cost; the FDA's approval workload would rise slightly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name and first-filer generic drug makers

drawbacks.text: The 180-day exclusivity is the main reward that pushes generic companies to challenge weak brand-name patents in court; letting the FDA approve competitors before the first filer launches could weaken that incentive and lead to fewer patent challenges that, once won, clear the market for all generics [S2].

A competing generic could still face later patent litigation even though the bill requires that no patent infringement claim currently blocks approval, so patients could see a generic pulled from the market mid-stream if a court later upholds a patent [S2] [S3].

The bill applies only to applications filed after enactment for drugs where no such certification was made before enactment, so it does nothing for generic situations already stuck under current law [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: this fixes one specific loophole — a first generic filer parking its exclusivity and locking everyone else out — and only after a long 33-month wait, with patent-related situations carved out. The main cost, a weaker incentive for first filers to challenge patents, is a legitimate trade-off that generic-policy experts generally acknowledge, though the bill's tight forfeiture rule for applicants who fail to launch suggests the sponsor tried to prevent abuse of the new pathway. On balance a modest, well-targeted pro-consumer fix rather than a sweeping drug-pricing measure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no vote, and no cosponsors since February 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Nikki Budzinski introduced the bill on February 6, 2025 [S1] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which handles drug approval law [S5].
The bill has attracted zero cosponsors, and the action history shows nothing after the referral [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers and first-filer generic companies keep the status quo: the first generic filer can still hold its 180-day exclusivity without launching, and no competing generic can be approved in the meantime. Patients waiting on those drugs continue paying brand-name prices longer than they otherwise would.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers holding unlaunched generic exclusivity

for.name: Rep. Nikki Budzinski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill — no markup, hearing, or vote appears in the action history since the February 2025 referral

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no member besides the sponsor has taken a position, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is not yet visible in the record.

industries.note: Brand manufacturers benefit when a first generic filer holds exclusivity without launching — including through patent settlements that delay generic entry — because the brand keeps its monopoly longer. This bill shortens that window by letting the FDA approve a competing generic after 33 months of inaction.

Companies that win the race to file first would lose the power to sit on their 180-day exclusivity indefinitely; a stalled filer would see competitors approved after 33 months, and a company that fails to launch within 75 days of approval forfeits that approval.
Generic makers stuck behind a first filer that never launched would gain a path to approval and market access, with a clear forfeiture rule if they themselves fail to launch within 75 days.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to House committee never receive a vote, and this one shows no momentum — zero cosponsors and no committee action in its first months. Its most realistic path to law is being folded into a larger Food and Drug Administration or prescription-drug package rather than moving on its own; left alone, it will likely sit in committee until the Congress ends in early 2027.
